items.original_title: Your Policyholder Has an AI Agent, Too
items.rss_title: Your Policyholder Has an AI Agent, Too
items.rss_description: Your Policyholder Has an AI Agent, Too AI & Machine Learning ITL Editorial Team Wed, 10/28/2026 - 16:09 Life insurers are AI. The next challenge is preparing for policyholders who use AI to understand, question and optimize their policies. November 5, 2026 Image Imagine the customer of a 20-year-old life insurance policy trying to figure out if it makes sense to surrender the policy. Do they call the insurance company first, hoping to talk to a knowledgeable agent? Probably not. They will upload the policy contract, riders and most recent statement to the AI assistant with a list of questions: What benefits would be lost by surrendering the policy? What happens to the outstanding loans? Are there other alternatives to surrendering the policy? Which policy provisions are the most important to consider before deciding? This AI might be right, or might be partly right, or might be very wrong. But what is becoming abundantly clear is that this customer arrives at their insurer with a level of analysis and a body of knowledge that once cost time, or cost money, or both. This leads me back to the question insurers have been asking for years about how AI will change what we do: underwriting, servicing, operations, all inside the enterprise. So what happens when the policyholder is AI-enabled as well? The information gap is starting to change The Society of Actuaries Research Institute is now seeking research on policyholder behavior in the artificial intelligence era. According to the proposal request, it is possible for consumers to use AI to understand a policy's provisions better to improve their premiums, loans and withdrawals, and claims through improved product features. That isn't proof that AI has changed lapse rates, loan behavior, or benefit usage yet. It's on the research agenda. The difference is significant. But the formal asking of such questions by the actuarial community indicates that consumer AI requires attention before the results become apparent in experience studies. Up until recently, this has created a bit of a predicament: an insurer has product specialists, actuaries, underwriters, policy administration systems, and decades of institutional knowledge; a policyholder has a lengthy contract written in technical language and maybe the occasion to review it a couple of times. Generative AI won't remove that imbalance entirely, but it certainly lowers the cost of asking sophisticated questions about a complex contract. That alone changes the dynamic of that interaction. A long-lived contract can meet a very different customer Life insurance is unique because the contract could go on for decades, and the technology available to the user would be different from the present one. A policy issued in the age of paper statements and telephone calls may one day be managed by a consumer carrying a persistence layer of AI that summarizes documents, compares alternatives, remembers every previous conversation, and prepares detailed questions before every interaction. The policy's bones haven't altered one bit. But a policyholder's ability to kick the tires and check them out has. All this matters because many decisions and actions can occur throughout the lifecycle of a single life insurance policy: premium payment policy, loans, withdrawals, changes of beneficiary, conversion, surrender, and more. By making those decisions easier to understand and execute throughout the life of the product, there's no guarantee that customer behavior in the future will continue to be like the historical behaviors that informed product assumptions. Policyholder behavior may become an AI issue SOA's current research request explicitly identifies potential effects on lapses, loans, withdrawals, and benefit usage. A separate 2026 SOA call for essays on AI and the potential for antiselection in life insurance distribution asks whether AI could help applicants or intermediaries anticipate underwriting outcomes, compare carriers, select underwriting pathways and apply sophisticated placement strategies at greater scale. Once more, these are questions under investigation, not established outcomes. But, one thing appears clear: certain presumptions in life insurance are based on how people behave. Making it easier to evaluate the timing and consequences of a lapse, loan, withdrawal, conversion, surrender, or benefit election changes behavior in ways that historical behavior doesn't predict. The negative reaction to that realization is to predict material disruption. The right reaction is to begin measuring whether AI-assisted behavior is emerging, where it's concentrated, and if it's big enough to matter. From a more strategic perspective, for our actuarial and product teams, consumer AI could one day become another behavioral variable to study, rather than just a way to service customers better. AI-enabled policyholders can also be good for insurers This should not be framed only as a new risk. When a customer understands the policy, it allows them to ask the right questions, know what benefits they have, prepare the right documents, and know what decision they are making. Beneficiaries will use AI to organize materials for a claim, point out relevant policy language, and understand what the insurer is asking for. A policyholder who walks up to the window to service their policy will know the difference between a loan, withdrawal, and a surrender. This is consistent with the financial services research. In July 2026, LIMRA reported that AI is increasingly being studied not only as a tool that assists advisors but as a potential source of analysis and financial guidance directly to consumers. While more knowledgeable buyers are good for insurers, they also bring heightened expectations. A customer who has just received an instantaneous explanation of a policy provision may be less patient about waiting for days to get a generic response from a service agent. The customer's AI is not the insurer's AI Yet there is a boundary—the policyholder's AI is outside of the insurer's control. The model was not chosen, trained, fed, or even provided with its system prompt by the insurer. Your AI could be reading an outdated contract, skipping an endorsement, not grasping a rider, getting guaranteed vs. non-guaranteed values mixed up, or just making up a provision out of whole cloth that does not exist. The assertion could be false, or at least inaccurate. The enterprise response is to make verifying what the authoritative policy information says more accessible. Suppose a customer says, "My AI says this rider gives me a different option." It should be easy for a service person to say, "Let's review what your current contract and its effective endorsements, transaction history, and applicable rules say about this." The more external AI becomes part of customer decision-making, the more valuable clear, accessible, and authoritative policy context becomes. Soon, the customer may send the AI instead The next step is not difficult to imagine: the policyholder does not merely use AI before contacting the insurer. The AI contacts the insurer. That scenario is beginning to appear in insurance discussions already. An October 2026 Insurance Thought Leadership article described consumer AI agents calling insurers and other businesses on behalf of users. At the same time, NIST is developing work around identity and authorization for software and AI agents as agent-to-agent interactions move from concept toward practical infrastructure. This brings us to a much bigger question for life insurers: what if a chatbot does work? How would your service channel know that it's talking to software working for a policyholder? What data could be returned through that channel? What happens when a customer AI and your system don't agree on a policy provision? When does it become important to switch the interaction over to a person? There's nothing in those two scenarios that necessitates banning the use of AI in customer service. It just means that we, as users of these services, will need to create different channels for them to go through. Build policyholder AI readiness Insurers do not need to predict exactly how fast consumer agents will mature, but they do need to prepare for the direction of travel. First, make authoritative policy context easier to retrieve and explain. A policyholder's AI will only be as useful as the documents and information it can access. Clear digital contracts, current riders, transaction history, and understandable definitions reduce the chance that outside AI starts from incomplete context. Next, test servicing journeys with customers being assisted by AI in mind. When customers arrive having 10 specific questions, they should not follow the same process as someone who has only general questions. Third, watch how behavior changes. Teams — actuarial, product, servicing — that rely on lapses, loans, withdrawals, conversions, benefit usage, and channel usage need to understand what constitutes a significant deviation. We want to avoid blaming AI if another force is at work. The goal is to build evidence that indicates that AI is a cause before rewriting our assumptions about behavior. Fourth, prepare digital channels for external agents. Identity, consent, disclosure and escalation will become practical. We do not want to automatically trust an outside agent. We do want to ensure legitimate customer assistance can reach us and not diminish customer protection. The next AI transformation may happen outside the insurer When asked about the insurance AI strategy, carriers invariably identify the same things: automated underwriting, automated servicing, automated claims, automated document processing, and automated decision support. However, when it comes to the impact of artificial intelligence on enhancing service innovation, customer capabilities are also affected. The increased understanding could allow them to compare things to other products, which could open them up to asking difficult questions. However, what I think we have not talked about and probably is an elephant in the room is that insurers are not going to be in control of all this. They can only prepare for it. Will the next phase of life insurance AI be defined by how intelligent the insurer becomes? Or by what happens when the policyholder becomes intelligent at machine speed? Bhargavi Vepuri

items.title: How Gen AI Can Help Shape Strategy
items.original_title: How Gen AI Can Help Shape Strategy
items.rss_title: How Gen AI Can Help Shape Strategy
items.rss_description: How Gen AI Can Help Shape Strategy PaulCarroll Mon, 11/02/2026 - 11:30 Bill Gates recently said he is using generative AI as part of the annual, two-week strategy session that determines how the Gates Foundation spends its next $10 billion. He'll be "taking the strategy notes and actually engaging in a dialogue with ChatGPT, Claude, Copilot, and even having them talk with each other," he said. I don't have $10 billion that I'm considering how to spend, and you may not, either, but genAI has now improved to the point where it can at least be an aid in setting strategy at almost any level. An old boss, Mel Bergstein, used to say: "Strategy is what you don't do." The idea worked for Mel, who founded a consulting firm, Diamond Management & Technology Partners, that pioneered the notion of digital strategy in the mid-1990s. Chunka Mui and I took Mel's adage further in our book, "Billion Dollar Lessons," for which we had 20 researchers spend two years looking at 2,500 major failures to identify the warning signs. Our recommended solution boiled down to having a "devil's advocate" identify all the underlying assumptions for a strategy, to keep problems from being glossed over as an executive team rushed to realize the CEO's plan. GenAI, used right, can now do a pretty good job of filling that role for anyone. Let's have a look. Gates told the New York Times that, "i n a few of the reviews, we’ll actually have the A.I. sit in. In a few cases, we’ll tell it: Hey, only speak if we ask you. And then in a few other cases, we’ll say: Hey, if you hear something you think is wrong or you hear us thinking about, for example, what are these statistics? Please engage. So we’ve gone from it being a joke [when someone suggested using genAI a year ago] to it will be a peer — not making any final decisions, but it will be a peer in deep, complex strategic discussions, making a significant contribution." I'm not willing to go that far just yet, partly because I'd need to test the domain knowledge that the large language models have about a subtle, heavily regulated business like insurance and partly because genAI has shown itself to be a sycophant. The biggest, overarching pattern of failure that Chunka and I found in the research for " Billion Dollar Lessons " was that people were reluctant to point out obvious problems that could derail initiatives that had the imprimatur of the CEO, and we don't want to replace human sycophants with AI ones. But you can describe your strategy to an AI, then pepper it with questions, going deeper each time while demanding evidence for its thinking and insisting it be blunt. Let's say you're thinking of buying a company. You could start with a general question: What could go wrong? Then you probe. How will our competitors react? What if interest rates increase? The economy goes into recession? The war in Iran escalates? Will we actually be able to cross-sell to our customers? Will the efficiencies from scale be as great as we expect? Who's done something similar and had problems? What were the problems? And on and on and on. You can do the same exercise if you're thinking of a new line of business, a software overhaul, adopting AI chatbots — or if you want to explore the dangers of standing pat, of not undertaking a major initiative that is under consideration. Major corporations have staff do extensive analysis along the lines I'm suggesting and, in the case of a possible acquisition, draw on their investment banks for advice — but the bias is always toward acting. If the perception is that the CEO backs an idea, the staff strives to make it work, not to kill it. Investment banks only collect their hefty fees if the deal happens, so why would they recommend against it? When Chunka and I did a consulting project with a major company that was considering launching autonomous vehicles, we saw elaborate studies it had commissioned from consulting firms that said the robotaxi business was a slam dunk and that the first to enter would win big. That was more than eight years ago. It turned out, however, that the executives working on the AV project internally were aware of all the sorts of operational and safety issues that we've all seen play out and that have slowed the robotaxi rollout. Those concerns were brought to the surface in the interviews for our devil's advocate review. Warren Buffett used to set aside two, equal pots of money when asking investment banks for advice on possible acquisitions — one for a bank that argued in favor of a deal and one for a bank that argued against it. Whichever carried the day collected its fees, while the other got nothing. You can be sure the "anti" bank worked as hard as possible on its arguments and evidence. In my experience, many big ideas should fall apart at the slightest scrutiny. As we wrote in "Billion Dollar Lessons," we thought 47% of the failures we investigated were based on strategies that never should have made it out of the strategy room — and not because those involved were stupid or inexperienced. The fifth-biggest cement maker in the world reasoned that it was really in the home products business because so much of its cement was used there. It began also making furnaces and lawn mowers... then went bankrupt and was bought by a competitor. Avon decided that its core competency was its culture of caring — not, you know, its line of cosmetics and its devoted salesforce — so it bought a maker of medical equipment and an operator of retirement homes. It had no idea how to operate the new businesses and quickly sold them at a major loss. In the early days of fax machines, FedEx spent hundreds of millions of dollars to set up a business that would collect a document from you, drive it to the nearest office, fax it to the office nearest your destination, then drive the fax to the recipient. The company somehow missed that Moore's law would soon make the devices so inexpensive that every company would have its own. It may take time to learn how to use genAI to avoid costly strategic mistakes — and that's even before we start using it as broadly as Gates is planning to. You'll likely also need to introduce to the LLM information specific to your market, including regulatory issues that it likely doesn't have even as these models try to Hoover up everything available on the internet. Insurance is a complicated market. But I think we're now at the point where genAI can, if managed correctly, start to catch strategic errors. We won't get that 47% figure for obviously bad ideas down to zero, but even heading toward 40%, maybe even 33%, would mark real progress. Cheers, Paul Image Paul Carroll At any level of setting strategy, from the boardroom to the one-person agency, generative AI can bring assumptions to the surface, helping you see what NOT to do. items.rss_description: November 2026 ITL FOCUS: Pricing & Rating RyanMeyer Mon, 11/02/2026 - 12:00 ITL FOCUS is a monthly initiative featuring topics related to innovation in risk management and insurance. November 2, 2026 FROM THE EDITOR Pricing is one of the most consequential functions in insurance — and one of the least visible. Claims gets the headlines. Underwriting gets the scrutiny. But pricing sits quietly underneath both, shaping profitability across millions of policies through assumptions that can go stale faster than anyone realizes. For most carriers, the mechanics of pricing haven’t kept pace with how quickly the world is changing. A rate change approved today might not be live in the market for weeks or months, trapped behind policy administration release cycles that were never designed for the kind of volatility the industry is now dealing with — social inflation, rising repair costs, tariff pressure, and catastrophe losses that keep defying historical patterns. Kumarappan Sundaram has spent years working through these problems with P&C carriers as a Managing Director at PwC. He brings a technology practitioner’s perspective to a function that often gets treated as a back-office infrastructure problem rather than a strategic capability. He’s measured about where AI fits — distinguishing what is already delivering clear value from what remains genuinely unproven — and direct about the sequencing mistakes carriers make when they try to modernize pricing before the foundation is in place. His practical advice is worth taking seriously: Before reaching for advanced analytics or AI, measure how long it actually takes to get an approved rate change into the market. Most carriers have never done that math. The number, he suggests, tends to be illuminating. Read the full interview to find out why decoupling rating logic from the core policy system is the starting point most carriers skip, how modern pricing platforms are beginning to close the long-standing gap between pricing and underwriting, and where AI can genuinely change the work. Pricing at the Speed of the Market Paul Carroll, Editor-in-chief of Insurance Thought Leadership. Pricing gets far less attention than claims or underwriting, yet it is important. How is the pricing function being modernized in insurance? And how should it be? Kumarappan Sundaram, Managing Director, PwC US Pricing gets less attention partly because a lot of the work is infrastructure: platforms, data flows and deployment processes. It is not a front-office workflow that a new tool can visibly transform. Modernization can be uneven. Personal lines are well on their way. Commercial lines are earlier in the journey and still rely heavily on underwriter judgment and rating engines embedded in policy administration systems. How pricing should be modernized can largely be a question of sequence. The foundation comes first: decoupling rating from the policy admin system. At the moment, actuaries produce pricing logic, which they hand to IT, which embeds the logic in a rating engine that sits within a policy admin system. So, making a change to the pricing logic means waiting for a new release of the policy admin system. If you decouple, you can make changes to ratings as and when you want. Once you’ve decoupled, you should build reliable data flows and establish clear governance. You can then go to the next level of capabilities, like advanced analytics and AI. Let’s say you have a $10 billion book. You’re considering changing a particular rate factor from X to Y, maybe related to driver age. Advanced analytics can help you understand the impact of the rate change on the whole book. The actuaries can then decide whether to make that rate change. Carriers can help deploy and monitor pricing changes quickly and safely. Paul Carroll From a technology standpoint, what are the most important shifts in P&C pricing and rating? items.summary: November 2026 ITL FOCUS: Pricing & Rating RyanMeyer Mon, 11/02/2026 - 12:00 ITL FOCUS is a monthly initiative featuring topics related to innovation in risk management and insurance. November 2, 2026 FROM THE EDITOR Pricing is one of the most consequential functions in insurance — and one of the least visible. Claims gets the headlines. Underwriting gets the scrutiny. But pricing sits quietly underneath both, shaping profitability across millions of policies through assumptions that can go stale faster than anyone realizes. For most carriers, the mechanics of pricing haven’t kept pace with how quickly the world is changing. A rate change approved today might not be live in the market for weeks or months, trapped behind policy administration release cycles that were never designed for the kind of volatility the industry is now dealing with — social inflation, rising repair costs, tariff pressure, and catastrophe losses that keep defying historical patterns. Kumarappan Sundaram has spent years working through these problems with P&C carriers as a Managing Director at PwC. He brings a technology practitioner’s perspective to a function that often gets treated as a back-office infrastructure problem rather than a strategic capability. He’s measured about where AI fits — distinguishing what is already delivering clear value from what remains genuinely unproven — and direct about the sequencing mistakes carriers make when they try to modernize pricing before the foundation is in place. His practical advice is worth taking seriously: Before reaching for advanced analytics or AI, measure how long it actually takes to get an approved rate change into the market. Most carriers have never done that math. The number, he suggests, tends to be illuminating. Read the full interview to find out why decoupling rating logic from the core policy system is the starting point most carriers skip, how modern pricing platforms are beginning to close the long-standing gap between pricing and underwriting, and where AI can genuinely change the work. Pricing at the Speed of the Market Paul Carroll, Editor-in-chief of Insurance Thought Leadership. Pricing gets far less attention than claims or underwriting, yet it is important. How is the pricing function being modernized in insurance? And how should it be? Kumarappan Sundaram, Managing Director, PwC US Pricing gets less attention partly because a lot of the work is infrastructure: platforms, data flows and deployment processes. It is not a front-office workflow that a new tool can visibly transform. Modernization can be uneven. Personal lines are well on their way. Commercial lines are earlier in the journey and still rely heavily on underwriter judgment and rating engines embedded in policy administration systems. How pricing should be modernized can largely be a question of sequence. The foundation comes first: decoupling rating from the policy admin system. At the moment, actuaries produce pricing logic, which they hand to IT, which embeds the logic in a rating engine that sits within a policy admin system. So, making a change to the pricing logic means waiting for a new release of the policy admin system. If you decouple, you can make changes to ratings as and when you want. Once you’ve decoupled, you should build reliable data flows and establish clear governance. You can then go to the next level of capabilities, like advanced analytics and AI. Let’s say you have a $10 billion book. You’re considering changing a particular rate factor from X to Y, maybe related to driver age. Advanced analytics can help you understand the impact of the rate change on the whole book. The actuaries can then decide whether to make that rate change. Carriers can help deploy and monitor pricing changes quickly and safely. Paul Carroll From a technology standpoint, what are the most important shifts in P&C pricing and rating? items.title: Why Can't We Fund Prevention?
items.original_title: Why Can't We Fund Prevention?
items.rss_title: Why Can't We Fund Prevention?
items.rss_description: Why Can't We Fund Prevention? Predict & Prevent ITL Editorial Team Wed, 11/04/2026 - 09:29 Industrial organizations excel at financing recovery from asset failures but struggle to justify prevention spending with the same economic rigor. November 5, 2026 Image We've built an extraordinarily sophisticated financial system around industrial failure. We can price it, insure it, reserve capital for it, and finance recovery when it happens, but preventing that same failure often requires an entirely different standard of proof. Insurance is exceptionally good at mobilizing money after something goes wrong. Natural catastrophes caused an estimated $100 billion in economic losses in the first half of 2026. Insurance covered approximately 42%, leaving nearly $60 billion to be absorbed elsewhere. Insurance's ability to fund recovery is indispensable. The shortfall also exposes a contradiction in how risk is funded. Premiums, deductibles, and recovery costs have established places in corporate budgets. A proposal to prevent an asset failure faces a tougher test. Someone must prove the threat is serious, determine what intervention it warrants, and defend spending money on an event that might never happen. Failure has a funding mechanism. Prevention has a business case to make. Insurance can transfer part of a financial loss. It cannot restore missed production, repair damaged customer relationships, or undo the wider consequences of an industrial disruption. The challenge is making prevention as intelligible and investable as recovery. Knowing the risk isn't the same as managing it Industrial organizations rarely lack information. They receive risk-engineering reports, inspection findings, maintenance records and alerts from connected equipment. Yet information doesn't guarantee action. A temperature change, unusual vibration, or a deteriorating component has little meaning in isolation. Its significance depends on the asset's role in the operation. Is there redundancy? What production depends on it? What would a shutdown cost? Could a failure disrupt customers, supply chains or other facilities? These questions turn technical observations into business consequences. Without that translation, recommendations can remain in reports while maintenance teams address more immediate demands and capital committees fund projects with clearer returns. Industry has invested heavily in detecting changing conditions and predicting potential failures. Those capabilities matter. Still, knowing what might fail doesn't tell an organization which emerging risks deserve attention first. A relatively minor condition on a critical asset may represent far greater exposure than a severe condition on equipment with sufficient redundancy. The challenge is understanding what matters most, what the consequences could be, and where intervention will create the greatest value. Prevention needs to compete for capital Consider a manufacturer that identifies deterioration in a critical component on its main production line. Although the component hasn't failed, its condition is changing. The organization must compare the cost of replacing it during a planned shutdown with the lost output, repair time, and disruption that could follow an unplanned failure. The consequences, however, may extend well beyond that production line. A shutdown could affect customer deliveries, contractual commitments, supply-chain continuity and financial performance. What appears to be a maintenance decision may represent a much larger business risk. The appropriate response might be immediate repair, closer monitoring, a change in operating parameters or acceptance of the exposure. Someone must have the authority to make that decision and commit the necessary resources before the opportunity to intervene passes. Now multiply that challenge across hundreds of assets and facilities, each presenting different levels of exposure. The question is no longer simply whether an individual intervention is justified. It's which interventions deserve priority when resources are limited, and the consequences extend across the enterprise. For decades, industry has developed sophisticated ways to measure losses after they occur. We need comparable discipline in understanding the economic value of preventing those losses before they happen. Capital should not only be deployed to absorb loss. It should be possible to direct it intelligently toward preventing loss. The standard for resilience must rise Risk assessments, inspections and engineering recommendations are essential. Completing those processes, however, doesn't necessarily mean an organization has addressed its most consequential exposures. An inspection can establish that a process was followed. A risk assessment can document a vulnerability. Neither, by itself, demonstrates that the organization is becoming more resilient. Industrial risk isn't static. Asset conditions change, operational dependencies evolve, and an exposure that appeared manageable during a periodic assessment may become significantly more consequential. A recommendation without a named decision-maker and deadline is information, not control. Someone must have the authority to accept the exposure, fund the response or explain why another course is justified. Following the process is important, although it's not the same as preventing the loss. Insurance can help change the economics of prevention Insurers can make recommendations easier to act on by explaining the severity and urgency of an exposure, not simply recording that it exists. Brokers can connect risk-engineering findings with an organization's insurance and resilience priorities. Operators must determine whether to intervene or accept the exposure and take responsibility for the outcome. There is also a bigger opportunity here. Insurers and brokers possess extraordinary expertise in understanding, quantifying, and pricing risk. Much of that expertise has historically helped organizations prepare financially for potential losses. What if more of it could be applied to making prevention economically compelling before those losses occur? Imagine insurers, brokers, and industrial operators working from a more continuous, consequence-based understanding of emerging physical risk. Rather than relying primarily on historical losses and periodic assessments, they could better understand where exposure is developing, which conditions present the greatest business consequences, and where intervention could materially reduce risk. This wouldn't eliminate uncertainty or diminish the need for insurance. It could, however, create a stronger economic foundation for prevention and a more productive relationship between risk financing and operational decision-making. For decades, the insurance industry has helped businesses understand the financial consequences of what can go wrong. That expertise will remain indispensable, but the next opportunity is to help make the economics of what doesn't have to go wrong equally visible. We've become extraordinarily good at financing industrial failure. It's time to become just as disciplined about investing in its prevention. Andy Pruett

items.extracted_text: Munich Re’s P&C reinsurance sees decline in Q3, while net result rises to €5.7bn for 9M’26 - Artemis.bm Munich Re’s P&C reinsurance sees decline in Q3, while net result rises to €5.7bn for 9M’26 - Artemis.bm Munich Re’s P&C reinsurance sees decline in Q3, while net result rises to €5.7bn for 9M’26 12th November 2026 - Author: Jack Willard Global reinsurer Munich Re has posted a lower net result of €1.742 billion for the third quarter of 2026, and a higher result of €5.667 billion for the first nine months of the year, while the firm’s P&C reinsurance arm saw a notable year-on-year decline as a result of currency and renewal effects. Back in October, Munich Re posted preliminary results for both the third quarter and nine-month period, which revealed a notable uplift to its full-year net profit guidance from €6.3 billion to €6.6 billion following the strong performance the reinsurance giant has delivered so far in the year. Today, Munich Re has posted its full financial results for both periods, reporting a net result of €1.742 billion in Q3’26, slightly down on the prior year’s €1.997 billion, and €5.667 billion for 9M’26, much higher than the previous year’s €5.176 billion. The reinsurer explained that the result was driven by a very pleasing operating performance across all business segments, and below-average major losses in property & casualty reinsurance At the same time, the reinsurer reported Group insurance revenue from insurance contracts issued of €16.626 billion in Q3’26, compared with €14.575 billion in Q3’25, and €46.583 billion for 9M’26 compared with €45.162 billion in 9M’25. All in all, for Q3, the total technical result amounted to €2.375 billion from €2.822 billion last year, while the operating result fell to €2.472 billion from €3.036 billion. Turning towards the reinsurance segment, the net result decreased to €1.479 billion in Q3’26 from €1.693 billion in the prior year quarter. However, the nine-month period saw a notable increase to €4.849 billion from €4.380 billion in 2025. In addition, Munich Re’s P&C reinsurance business generated a net result of €938 million in the third quarter of 2026, compared with €1.187 billion in the prior year period, as insurance revenue from insurance contracts issued increased to €4.446 billion from €4.241 billion in Q3’25. The firm’s P&C reinsurance combined ratio was 80% this quarter, up on the prior year’s 62.7% as a result of higher major losses year-on-year. As mentioned, Munich Re says that the year-on-year revenue decline in P&C reinsurance to €12.4 billion for 9M’26 is a result of currency and renewal effects. Munich Re also reported that major losses amounted to €646 million in third quarter of 2026 after retrocession and before tax, including run-off profits and losses for major claims from previous years. This compares to Q3’25, where reported major losses were just €118 million. The reinsurer announced that natural disaster losses totalled €514 million in Q3’26, with the costliest event being the El Choco earthquake in Colombia at a cost of €300 million. Overall, major-loss expenditure amounted to 14.9% of net insurance revenue, below the expected 18% but higher than the 2.9% recorded last year. “Munich Re achieved profitable growth in the first nine months of the year. The Group’s net result and insurance revenue rose significantly year on year. In the third quarter, we benefited from low major-loss expenditure and expanded our business, particularly in less volatile segments such as life and health reinsurance. The increase in our profit target to €6.6bn reflects the very pleasing operating performance across all business segments. This broad diversification of our earnings drivers is a core component of our Ambition 2030 strategy and ensures Munich Re’s continued success,” commented Andrew Buchanan, Chief Financial Officer. As highlighted, Munich Re’s strong 9M’26 performance has led the reinsurer to lift its full year net result guidance by €300 million to €6.6 billion, while the company also anticipates that the net combined ratio in P&C reinsurance will amount to less than 80%. items.extracted_text: Zurich Insurance Says Europe Storms Drove Catastrophe Losses Article 0 Comments Zurich Insurance Group AG said it saw elevated natural catastrophe losses in its property/casualty business in the third quarter, following storms in Germany, Italy and Switzerland. The natural catastrophe loss ratio in the unit rose to 3.2% in the nine months to September, from 1.4% a year earlier, the Swiss insurer said in its third-quarter trading update on Thursday. The period was marked by weather events in Europe including hailstorms and heavy rain, which drove property, vehicle and infrastructure claims. An earthquake in Colombia also contributed to the jump. Zurich said pricing trends in its property and casualty business are moderating, amid slowing premium increases across the industry. Gross written premiums in the business rose to $42.1 billion, on a like-for-like basis a 7% increase compared to the previous year. Slower rate increases in the large-property business weighed on commercial insurance, Zurich said. In the life business, gross written premiums gained 3% with protection and unit-linked businesses seeing strong premium growth. Farmers Exchanges saw a 4% increase in dollar terms. Analysts at Jefferies said that the rate changes “positively surprised as prices are still up or flat” despite momentum slowing in some areas such as U.S. commercial. Shares were up 1.2% at 9:43 a.m. in Zurich. In October, Zurich completed its $11 billion acquisition of specialty insurer Beazley Plc., a deal it said would create the world’s largest specialty insurer with about $15 billion of gross written premiums. The Swiss firm said the deal would also help it leverage Beazley’s presence in the Lloyd’s of London market. The deal had sparked some concern that expert underwriters at the London-based firm would leave rather than be absorbed into the larger firm. Chief Executive Officer Mario Greco said on a media call Thursday that so far there had been “very little turnover at Beazley,” which in a normal year is 10% for underwriters. Although retention bonuses are being paid, Greco said that it is not just about the money but the opportunities and possibilities offered to them. The firm said it will provide an update on the integration of Beazley at its investor day on November 17. items.extracted_text: VKB lifts target to €200m for King Max Re German multi-peril cat bond renewal - Artemis.bm VKB lifts target to €200m for King Max Re German multi-peril cat bond renewal - Artemis.bm VKB lifts target to €200m for King Max Re German multi-peril cat bond renewal 11th November 2026 - Author: Jack Willard German domestic market insurance group VKB is now aiming to upsize its latest catastrophe bond deal, raising the target size to secure a slightly larger €200 million of German multi-peril reinsurance protection from the King Max Re II DAC (Series 2026-1) issuance, this publication has learned. Versicherungskammer Bayern Versicherungsanstalt des oeffentlichen Rechts’ (VKB) made its return to the catastrophe bond market in October to sponsor its second cat bond deal. As we’ve explained before, this transaction is a renewal of sorts for the company’s soon to mature debut cat bond, the €175 million King Max Re DAC 2023 , which is scheduled to mature in early January 2027. Initially VKB was looking to secure €175 million of multi-peril reinsurance with this King Max Re II Series 2026-1 deal, which would fully replace the expiring cat bond protection. In our first update on this transaction, we learned that VKB was aiming to secure its latest catastrophe bond deal at reduced pricing as the spread guidance for the notes on offer for this issuance was reduced. Now, we’ve been told that VKB is looking to secure more German multi-peril reinsurance protection from investors, with the target for this King Max Re II DAC (Series 2026-1) deal now raised to €200 million. King Max Re II DAC is now offering a single €200 million tranche of King Max Re II Series 2026-1 Class A notes to cat bond investors, which are designed to provide sponsoring reinsurer VKB Re with indemnity and per-occurrence triggered reinsurance protection against losses from a range of perils, including earthquake, hailstorm, flood and windstorm in Germany, running across a three year term beginning January 1st 2027. The now €200 million King Max Re II Series 2026-1 Class A cat bond notes come with an initial expected loss of 1.68%. items.title: The Flaw in 'Human-in-the-Loop'
items.original_title: The Flaw in 'Human-in-the-Loop'
items.rss_title: The Flaw in 'Human-in-the-Loop'
items.rss_description: The Flaw in 'Human-in-the-Loop' PaulCarroll Tue, 11/10/2026 - 12:55 The notion that there must always be a "human in the loop" has become de rigueur in any discussion of AI implementation in business. The cynical side of me suspects that part of the reason is to reassure everyone that AI won't lead to mass layoffs, but there are also plenty of practical reasons to have humans check the work of AIs. Or maybe not. At least not for long. A recent article in Harvard Business Review argues that human supervisors quickly become numb and simply approve the recommendations of the AI as it becomes increasingly accurate. And I think the author has a point, based on what I've seen of human/AI interactions in semi-autonomous cars. There needs to be a better way. Let's have a look. Early in the development of its driverless cars, Google gave demo models to employees. Google warned them that the AI wasn't perfect and instructed them to have their hands on the wheel, always ready to take control. That worked... for a little while. A very little while. As the AI proved to be reliable, the drivers began to relax their hold on the wheel, then started to take their eyes off the road, then began reading or looking at their phones. When the car signaled that the drivers had to take over, they needed perhaps 10 seconds to fully reengage. Given that a car going 60mph travels nearly 300 yards in 10 seconds, Google realized its hybrid approach wouldn't work and committed to producing only cars that could be fully autonomous. Other makers of autonomous vehicles, most notably Tesla, continue to offer cars that take a hybrid, human/AI approach, but I think that's irresponsible (as I wrote at length a year ago). Now, an article in Harvard Business Review offers a similar view about the dangers of having a "human in the loop" to supervise work done by AIs. The author, a senior fellow at Cal, writes: "Decades of research on automation show that better automation systems lead to worse human safety layers; as automation grows more reliable, the people monitoring it grow complacent, their skills atrophy, and they become less attentive.... AI compounds the problem. Its failures sound as confident, fluent, and well-structured as its successes.... "Even when validation works and people catch errors, every correction is captured as training data. Each exception a person handles teaches the system to handle that exception; the better the data, the smaller the scope of human validation needed in the future." The article says the lack of reliability of the humans in the loop is actually just the start of the problem. He writes: "The larger problem with the human-in-the-loop organization, though, is that the entire blueprint reads the transformation backwards. It organizes the company around the shrinking frontier of what machines can’t yet do. But there’s a larger opportunity here. Because AI removes constraints, it enables new combinations of work, new decision rights, and new forms of value. Organizations, accordingly, have an opportunity to reorganize and 'rebundle' around those new decisions rather than the shrinking residue of the old work." He goes on to lay out how to think about rebundling: "Instead of asking which tasks the machine can take over, leading organizations should ask which new roles the technology makes possible, and then redesign the organization around them." He lists several steps that can lead you to new approaches, which seem intriguing and which you may want to explore. For now, though, I just want to make the point that "human in the loop" isn't a panacea, certainly not in the long term. The reviewers of AI work can quickly become as reliant on the AI as those Google employees who found themselves with their hands off the wheel, their eyes off the road and their minds far away from driving when a problem popped up in front of them. Cheers, Paul Image Paul Carroll An HBR article argues that human supervisors quickly become unreliable as the AI becomes increasingly accurate. items.extracted_text: US Sues Lyft, Alleges Discrimination Against Disabled Riders Article 0 Comments The U.S. Justice Department sued Lyft on Monday, alleging the ride-hailing services provider discriminated against passengers with disabilities, including those who use service animals and mobility devices such as stowable wheelchairs. The lawsuit seeks $53 million for individuals with disabilities whom Lyft allegedly discriminated against, and who have submitted complaints to Lyft or the Department of Justice, the DOJ said in a statement. Lyft said it disagreed with the allegations made in the Justice Department lawsuit that was filed in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California. The lawsuit alleges Lyft violated Title III of the Americans with Disabilities Act of 1990, which prohibits private transportation companies from discriminating based on disability. The lawsuit seeks a court order to force Lyft to stop the alleged discrimination, to modify its policies to comply with the Americans with Disabilities Act, and to train its staff and drivers on the law, the Justice Department said. The Justice Department alleged that Lyft and its drivers routinely refuse service to individuals with disabilities and refuse to reasonably modify Lyft’s policies and practices to avoid such discrimination. “We have long-standing policies requiring drivers to accommodate riders who travel with service animals or use foldable mobility devices, and drivers who violate these policies face serious consequences, including permanent deactivation,” Lyft said in a statement responding to the lawsuit. Lyft also said it has cooperated with the DOJ during its review. Last year, the U.S. government sued Uber, accusing the ride-sharing company of violating the same federal law by discriminating against passengers with disabilities. That lawsuit sought $125 million for individuals subjected to the alleged discrimination and who previously submitted complaints to Uber or the Justice Department. Uber had said it disagreed with all of the allegations, and was committed to expanding access and improving the experience of riders with disabilities. items.extracted_text: Ferma president rejects need for standalone AI insurance - Commercial Risk Ferma president Philippe Ferma president Philippe Cotelle has called on insurers to clarify how artificial intelligence (AI) risks are addressed across existing insurance policies, rather than seeking to develop a standalone AI insurance product. Cotelle told Commercial Risk’s Global Programmes Europe conference that the rapid adoption of AI by business is creating uncertainty about whether the risks are adequately covered by existing insurance policies. He said currently the situation is unclear. “If I ask risk managers if they are covered for the consequences of AI, the answer is grey or maybe. We cannot live with that uncertainty. We need to make sure that this evolution is taken on board by the insurance market,” he said at the event partnered by Marsh, Aon, QBE, AIG, HDI Global, Generali, Intact Insurance, BHSI and Risk FabrIQ Cotelle warned against AI exclusions because organisations will look for different partners if insurers are unable to provide the support needed. But, equally, he is against a dedicated AI insurance line, arguing that this could create coverage gaps. “I don’t think proposals for a new AI liability coverage are a good idea. It is not a good idea because if you have a dedicated AI coverage there will be an exclusion in your general liability coverage somewhere. Then you have problems ensuring there are no gaps in cover,” said Ferma’s president. Instead, Cotelle believes insurers should better assess the use of AI and factor that into underwriting decisions across the various lines of insurance, using their influence to encourage better governance and risk management. “On the property side insurers promote the use of sprinklers and this best practice has an impact on the underwriting process. So if you have a building with no sprinkler maybe you will not find insurance or your insurance will be more expensive, or maybe the limit will be different. That is exactly the sort of thing that we need to put in place for AI,” he said. Over time, this would encourage organisations to improve their AI risk management practices, while giving insurers a clearer understanding of the risks, added Ferma’s president. “And that should drive, slowly, risk improvements,” he said. Cotelle said this path forward would allow insurers to play an active role in supporting the adoption of AI, while ensuring that the associated risks are properly understood and addressed across the wider insurance programme. items.extracted_text: Cat bond market breadth expands, issuance concentrates in 1% to 3% EL range: Euler ILS Partners - Artemis.bm Cat bond market breadth expands, issuance concentrates in 1% to 3% EL range: Euler ILS Partners - Artemis.bm Cat bond market breadth expands, issuance concentrates in 1% to 3% EL range: Euler ILS Partners 12th November 2026 - Author: Steve Evans Through the recent period of brisk issuance the catastrophe bond market has been expanding rapidly, with now 20% more cat bond deals available to investors than a year ago, analysis from specialist Swiss insurance-linked securities investment manager Euler ILS Partners shows. In its review of the market after the third-quarter of 2026, Euler ILS Partners found that the size of the market had increased 17.3% year-on-year, while the number of deals outstanding rose slightly faster by 20% to reach 402. This expansion in market breadth means more individual investment opportunities are available to cat bond fund managers and investors, which helps in portfolio construction and diversification. But the metrics speak to a softening marketplace, with the average coupon of the cat bond market down 9.2% at 7.14% and the average spread down faster with a 21.6% decline YoY to 5.05%. The market has seen its issuance increasingly concentrated in the 1% to 3% expected loss range, Euler ILS Partners noted, which has raised the average expected loss of outstanding catastrophe bonds by 12.5% YoY to 2.4%. Euler ILS Partners’ data previously showed the average expected loss of the cat bond market had risen from 2.29% at the end of Q1 2026 to 2.31% by the end of the second-quarter , so the increase has continued. Euler ILS Partners commented as to how the market’s expected loss has developed, saying, “The share of issuance in the 1% to 3% expected-loss range increased from 37% in 2018 to 64% in 2026 YTD. As a result, lower-EL layers have become less prevalent in new issuance.” You can see how expected losses of catastrophe bond issuance have developed by year in the chart below, which shows the weighted average across 2026 issuance so far at 2.67%. Unweighted, Artemis’ data on catastrophe bond issuance expected losses shows the average at 2.85% in 2026 to-date, which is now the highest level since 2019 . Euler ILS Partners chart (above) shows issuance contracting fastest in the 1% to 2% EL range and increasing in the 2% to 3% range, which suggests the weighted average may increase further as this year progresses. Through reinsurance market cycles the average expected loss of cat bond issuance tends to rise when prices soften, as sponsors capitalise on being able to bring higher-risk deals to market. At the same time, through the third-quarter of 2026 the composition of perils in the cat bond market remained relatively stable according to Euler ILS Partners’ data. US hurricane risk still accounts for around 75% of exposure after Q3, so flat with the end of Q2 figure, but up from 74% as of the end of Q1. items.extracted_text: El Niño’s Odds of Being Worst Ever Edge Lower, US Climate Prediction Center Says Article 0 Comments The odds are slipping that the “super” El Niño reshaping global weather patterns will be a record breaker, according to a new outlook from the leading US forecaster. The chances that the El Niño spawned by unusually warm seas in the tropical Pacific Ocean will be stronger than the 1982-1983 season have dropped to roughly 60% from a previous forecast of 83%, the US Climate Prediction Center said Thursday. The early ’80s event was the most severe in records dating back to 1950, based on a rolling, three-month average of ocean-temperature readings. No matter where the current pattern ultimately ranks, it remains a dire portent of potentially disastrous weather anomalies that would threaten life and property on multiple continents. Weather models now indicate that the ocean may begin to cool rapidly as wind patterns shift in early 2027. El Niño is expected to fade heading into the Northern Hemisphere summer, with odds of a La Niña outbreak rising to more than 30% during the June-to-August time frame. Related: El Niño and Heat Fuel Destructive Storms Across Pacific Ocean A fast transition from El Niño to La Niña can create significant risks, including an enhanced fire threat in Southern California. Plants and grasses that flourished around Los Angeles during the wet El Niño winter of 2023-2024 helped fuel devastating fires in 2025 amid a hot, dry La Niña event. The current El Niño has contributed to an explosion of powerful Pacific typhoons and hurricanes. High winds, damaging waves and surging tides have wreaked havoc on ports and coastal communities from Japan and Taiwan to San Francisco and Long Beach , California. Read More: Powerful El Niño Nears Record Strength, US Forecasters Say Farmers in Southeast Asia, India and parts of Africa, meanwhile, are contending with unusually poor rains that threaten to dent yields. Disruptive fires in Indonesia that have blanketed the surrounding region in haze are finally easing as wet weather returns. items.extracted_text: Uninsured And Flooded Out, A Colorado Man Worries If Life Will Be Normal Again Article 0 Comments Matthew Martinez has lived nearly all of his 60 years in a canyon on the Navajo River and had never seen severe floods. Then, twice over the last two weeks, the river surged through his home and outbuildings in far southwestern Colorado, about 25 miles (40 kilometers) south of the resort town of Pagosa Springs. Now a horse is missing, his barn is damaged and the river swallowed a corral. The house is strewn with mud. His tools washed downstream. “We’re in trouble, all of us are. Not just me, everybody,” Martinez said through tears when he returned Wednesday. He said several families that go back 100 years in the same canyon had similar damage. “Nobody expected this.” The Navajo, San Juan and Animas rivers are among those that surged beyond their banks when round after round of storms dumped heavy rain across the Four Corners region of Arizona, Colorado, New Mexico and Utah. Scientists say a supercharged El Niño event — when warm water in the Pacific disrupts weather patterns — is making heavy rainfall more likely and increasingly intense across the South. Recent flooding has struck Flagstaff, Sedona and Tucson in Arizona Pagosa Springs and Durango in southwestern Colorado Farmington in northwestern New Mexico tiny Bluff in southeastern Utah parts of the vast Navajo Nation. With a break in the weather at last, some evacuees are returning home. For Martinez, who was out of town for knee surgery, getting back meant navigating a mucky mess with a four-wheel drive vehicle and a lot of patience over beaten gravel roads. And he’s finding his struggles may have just begun. Martinez said he doesn’t have flood insurance because insurers wouldn’t provide cover for a house so near the water. He estimates at least $200,000 in losses. He and his fiancée first stayed with one of his sons, then moved to a hotel. Both places subsequently flooded. Now they’re in an Airbnb, but he worries they could end up homeless when his emergency voucher runs out in a few days. “The government spends, you know, just millions and billions of money on overseas and everything. Right now we need that money on this side,” he said. “We need to get this, you know, all this put back together.” A FEMA representative came to his property and took photos after the first flood. The second flood hit three days later and was twice as bad, he said. “I know we’re on some list right now,” Martinez said. “So we’ll listen every day and we’ll see what options we have and go from there.” As he heals from the knee surgery, he’s considering whether he should ask family and friends for help cleaning up. Hauling debris to the dump would cost $300 per load and ultimately could total thousands of dollars he does not readily have, he said. The flooding did help end months of drought in the Four Corners area, but the raging torrents washed away rich topsoil on his land, leaving just sand and rock. Now he wonders how he’ll feed his remaining animals without pasture next year. “The normal might not ever be normal again,” Martinez said. Gruver reported from Fort Collins, Colorado. items.extracted_text: Chipmakers Warn AI Demand Is Creating Bottlenecks in Automotive Supply Chain Article 0 Comments Dutch chipmaker Nexperia is “totally oversubscribed” as suppliers divert manufacturing capacity toward fast-growing AI data centers and away from the mature chips used in cars and industrial equipment, interim CEO Stefan Tilger told Reuters at the Electronica trade fair in Munich on Tuesday. Tilger said some competitors had shifted capacity away from the commodity semiconductors supplied by Nexperia, creating bottlenecks in parts of the automotive supply chain. “The automotive industry is suffering at the moment quite heavily,” he said in an interview. STMicroelectronics CEO Jean-Marc Chery warned on Monday that foundries and chip-packaging companies were increasingly shifting resources away from products used in automotive and industrial applications. “We see many bottlenecks,” Chery said at a CEO panel ahead of the conference on Monday. The comments add to evidence that the AI investment boom is creating bottlenecks elsewhere in the semiconductor supply chain, as manufacturers prioritize higher-margin products linked to data centers and artificial intelligence. Some foundries and assembly and packaging firms that previously served a broad range of customers “are disengaging … from mainstream technology,” he said. Tilger said demand from AI data centers and robotics was absorbing capacity, while investment in the mature technologies used for diodes, transistors and other basic components had lagged for years. Nexperia specializes in high-volume, low-cost semiconductors used primarily in vehicles and industrial equipment. Unlike larger rivals such as STMicroelectronics, it has a narrower product range focused on mature-node components. Chery said ST’s own manufacturing footprint offered some protection from supply constraints. “We control a part of our future with our CapEx and our manufacturing,” he said. items.extracted_text: California Earthquake Authority lowers pricing again for still $900m Ursa Re 2026-1 cat bond - Artemis.bm California Earthquake Authority lowers pricing again for still $900m Ursa Re 2026-1 cat bond - Artemis.bm California Earthquake Authority lowers pricing again for still $900m Ursa Re 2026-1 cat bond 12th November 2026 - Author: Jack Willard The California Earthquake Authority’s (CEA) new Ursa Re Ltd. (Series 2026-1) catastrophe bond remains at the upsized $900 million target, but pricing has been lowered again for the notes on offer, as the company targets strong execution with its latest cat bond deal, Artemis understands. The California Earthquake Authority (CEA) is one of the most consistent sponsors of catastrophe bonds, with this marking the 25th cat bond sponsorship we have tracked from the insurer. View details of every catastrophe bond sponsored by the CEA in the Artemis Deal Directory . Initially, the CEA was aiming to secure $600 million of reinsurance protection from this Ursa Re 2026-1 cat bond sponsorship. In our first update on this transaction, we learned that the CEA was looking to increase the amount of reinsurance limit from its latest deal, with Ursa Re Ltd. offering $900 million of notes across the two tranches of this Series 2026-1 cat bond issuance, a 50% increase from the initial $600 million target. At the same time, the CEA also looked to capitalise on investor appetite within the market, as the spread guidance for both notes on offer for this deal were reduced. We’re told that the upsized $900 million target remains, but CEA is still seeking to secure that protection at a more cost-effective rate, as the price guidance has been lowered once again for each of the tranches on offer. As we’ve previously said, at a $900 million issuance size, Artemis’ data shows that this new cat bond for the CEA is targeted to become the company’s largest since 2017 and the earthquake insurers second largest cat bond sponsorship ever. Ursa Re Ltd. continues to offer $900 million of earthquake reinsurance limit across the two tranches of cat bond notes on offer. These notes will provide the CEA with a roughly four-year source of fully-collateralized California earthquake reinsurance protection on an indemnity trigger and annual aggregate basis, which is the same trigger structure that CEA’s cat bonds have adopted in the past. What was a $350 million tranche of Series 2026-1 Class D notes are still targeted at their increased $500 million in size we understand. These Class D notes have an initial expected loss of 2.68% and they initially offered to cat bond investors with price guidance in a range from 4% to 4.5%, which was first lowered to between 3.75% to 4%, and we’re now told have been lowered to a revised range of 3.5% to 3.75%. What was initially a $250 million tranche of Series 2026-1 Class H of notes are still targeted at their increased $400 million in size. The Class H notes come with an initial expected loss of 6.35% and were first offered to cat bond investors with price guidance in a range from 8.5% to 9.5%, which was later revised to lower spread of 8.25% to 8.5%. We’re now told this price guidance has been lowered once again, to a revised range of 8% to 8.25%. We’ve previously said that we believe the Class H notes have the highest expected loss for any tranche of catastrophe bonds that we have seen sponsored by the CEA. The CEA looks set to meaningfully capitalise on catastrophe bond market conditions, in being able to secure 50% more fully-collateralized California earthquake reinsurance protection than originally sought. The decline in pricing is also no surprise given how cat bond issues have been executing of late across the market, as the space remains well-capitalised. items.extracted_text: At Least 8 Killed, 17 Injured in NYC Multiple-Dwelling Building Collapse Article 0 Comments At least eight people have died and more than 17 including seven children and one firefighter have been injured in a building collapse in Brooklyn. The New York Fire Department (FDNY) responded within one minute to a 4:01 p.m. call Wednesday to 1321 Flatbush Avenue in Brooklyn for the collapse of a three-story, multiple-dwelling building into an adjacent construction evacuation site. More than 250 fire, police and other first responders including all K-9 units immediately began search-and-rescue operations that continued into last evening and this morning. New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani r eported this morning that last night’s death toll of two had risen to eight after emergency workers spent the night searching the debris for victims. “Multiple people from the building and the construction site were trapped,” FDNY Commissioner Lillian Bonsignore said during an 8:30 pm press briefing with the mayor and other city officials. “This will be a prolonged operation. Collapse operations are extremely dangerous. Every move is choreographed and critically important to patient outcomes and member safety. Members have been working methodically and haven’t stopped since they arrived this afternoon.” The numbers of people who were in the building or may still be trapped under debris are unknown. Mayor Mamdani said the buildings department and police will conduct an investigation into the cause. The city building commissioner said the construction workers were doing excavation work on the three-story site in anticipation of building a nine-story structure. FDNY officials said they are taking steps to prevent a secondary collapse of the adjacent building. The Red Cross, utility workers and all city emergency departments are involved in the rescue and recovery effort. “This has been a whole-of-government response. I want to thank the first responders who arrived in under a minute and have spent hours working in dangerous and highly technical conditions to rescue New Yorkers,” Mayor Mamdani stated. “Their courage and dedication are extraordinary.” Was this article valuable? items.extracted_text: ANZ CEO Matos Warns of Global Jobs Crisis Without AI Rules Article 0 Comments ANZ Group Holdings Ltd. Chief Executive Officer Nuno Matos has called for global regulation to manage the impact of artificial intelligence on the labor market, which he warned could trigger an international crisis. Should large-scale job cuts of up to 50% emerge, “we’ll have a crisis and it’s not going to be in Australia, it’s going to be a global crisis,” Matos said Thursday during a parliamentary hearing in Canberra. “This is one of the few examples where I would say some global regulation is needed to make sure that society does not go into trouble,” he said. The adoption of AI among Australia’s banks in recent years has coincided with job cuts amid a challenging economic backdrop. Skeptics including Australia’s finance sector union have accused banks of replacing staff with AI. Outside the finance sector, Canva Inc. this month announced a sweeping overhaul that will see 22% of its staff leave while Microsoft Corp. is offering buyouts to around a quarter of its 223,000 staff as part of the tech giant’s efforts to retool its workforce for the AI era. “I hope that obviously the world and the administrations are capable of cooperating and ensuring that this technology does not create a social problem at a global level,” Matos said. Matos said workers should develop AI skills to reduce the risk of losing their job to colleagues who are more proficient, and pointed to ANZ’s efforts to develop staff capacity internally. The comments intensify concerns Matos has previously voiced about the quickly developing technology, which he believes could be used to attack banks as key choke-points for the economy. “AI has a dark side,” he said. “Wide adoption of AI without having the adequate guardrails — it’s a big problem. No banks should be building AI without building the right controls,” he said, adding that ANZ is developing its own “control platform” as it employs the technology across the bank. ANZ is also using AI to prevent fraud and identify cyber weaknesses, he said. Photograph: ANZ CEO Nuno Matos photo credit: Brendon Thorne/Bloomberg Copyright 2026 Bloomberg. items.extracted_text: SafePoint’s $100m Nature Coast Re 2026-3 industry-loss cat bond price moves to upper-end - Artemis.bm SafePoint’s $100m Nature Coast Re 2026-3 industry-loss cat bond price moves to upper-end - Artemis.bm SafePoint’s $100m Nature Coast Re 2026-3 industry-loss cat bond price moves to upper-end 12th November 2026 - Author: Jack Willard SafePoint continues to target $100 million of annual aggregate and industry-loss index triggered named storm protection through its Arthur Re Ltd. – Nature Coast Re 2026-3 catastrophe bond deal, but we’re told the price guidance for the notes on offer has moved towards the upper-end of the initial range. As we’ve explained before, this is not the first time SafePoint Insurance Company has ventured to the catastrophe bond market to obtain securitized industry-loss warranty (ILW) type protection. In December 2024, the expansive US primary insurer secured $200 million of state-weighted, annual aggregate and industry loss index trigger reinsurance through sponsorship of a Nature Coast Re Ltd. (Series 2025-1) cat bond, which remains in-force until the end of 2028. The target issuance size for this Arthur Re Ltd. – Nature Coast Re 2026-3 catastrophe bond for SafePoint remains unchanged we are told, with still $100 million of annual aggregate and industry-loss index triggered named storm protection being sought from the capital markets for SafePoint. However, we’re told the price guidance has been updated and moved to the upper-end of initial guidance. For this index triggered cat bond, SafePoint is utilising Arthur Re Ltd., the Gallagher Re operated issuance platform developed by the broker to make industry-loss index trigger cat bonds more cost-effective and efficient. As we said in our first article on this transaction, the ceding company to this cat bond issuance is Pompano Re Ltd., a special purpose insurer (SPI) that SafePoint established back in 1999 , which now acts as a captive reinsurer for the insurer and its reciprocal underwriting entities. Arthur Re Ltd. continues to offer a $100 million tranche of Class A notes to cat bond investors on behalf of a segregated account named Nature Coast Re 2026-3. These Nature Coast Re 2026-3 cat bond notes are designed to provide Pompano Re with a multi-year source of fully-collateralized US named storm retrocessional reinsurance protection from the capital markets. That protection will be on an annual aggregate and industry loss index trigger basis. The notes will provide coverage across all 50 US states, along with DC and the US Virgin Islands. The protection will run across a roughly four-year term to the end of November 2030, with annual aggregate risk periods that cover four hurricane seasons for the sponsor. The single tranche of Class A Nature Coast Re 2026-3 notes will also feature a franchise deductible of $40 million, an attachment point at $450 million and exhaustion at $650 million (remember, this is based on index values not ground-up reported industry losses). These notes come with an initial attachment probability of 5.39% and an initial expected loss of 4.082% and were initially marketed to cat bond investors with price guidance for a spread of between 7.25% to 8%. We understand that the price guidance has been updated and moved to 8%, so the upper-end of the initial range, which demonstrates that cat bond investors remain disciplined and seek risk-commensurate returns for this transaction. SafePoint continues to utilise the catastrophe bond market throughout 2026. Back in February, the firm secured $250 million of indemnity protection from the Nature Coast Re Ltd. (Series 2026-1) cat bond. Then, just last week, the company managed to secure its largest catastrophe bond yet, as the Nature Coast Re Ltd. (Series 2026-2) deal was priced, providing the firm an upsized $650 million source of collateralized reinsurance protection, As a reminder, you can read all about this new Arthur Re Ltd. – Nature Coast Re 2026-3 catastrophe bond and every other cat bond transaction in the extensive Artemis Deal Directory .
